newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. says Iraqi leaders hindering arms inspections.
newsitem.headline: U.N. says Iraqi leaders hindering arms inspections.

text.p: Rolf Ekeus, the chief U.N. arms inspector, on Friday called on Iraqi President Saddam Hussein's government to abandon "once and for all" ambitions to retain or acquire weapons of mass destruction.

In a major half-year report to the Security Council, Ekeus said remaining problems in ridding Iraq of dangerous arms were not technical but political. He said Iraq too often had undercut the inspectors ability to do their jobs.
"Their solution requires a major political decision by Iraq's leadership to give up, once and for all, all capabilities and ambition to retain or acquire the proscribed weapons," he said.

Iraq, he said, on repeated occasions threatened to shoot down helicopters used by the commission if they did not follow certain routes. At times Iraqi helicopters had flown dangerously close and Iraq personnel on board "have attempted to wrest control of the aircraft."
Another example of obstruction was Iraq's National Monitoring Directorate (NMD), established as a liaison with the commission.

"When minders from the NMD escort the commmission's inspectors, they have often interrupted interviews and instructed Iraqi site personnel to provide wrong information or to refuse to answer relevant questions," Ekeus said.

A clean bill of health by Ekeus, head of the U.N. special commission on ridding Iraq of weapons of mass destruction, is a key requirement before the embargo on Iraqi oil exports can be lifted entirely. Iraq has been under U.N. sanctions since its invasion of Kuwait in August 1990.
The report also said Iraq was hindering the long-term monitoring system the commission set up to make sure Baghdad does not reacquire the dangerous arms.
"If the trend were not reversed it could result in a situation with political consequences, whereby monitoring could no longer be considered operational," Ekeus warned.

But Ekeus, who will be leaving his job before September to become Sweden's ambassador to Washington, said little remained unknown about Baghdad's nuclear, biological, chemical and ballistic missile potential, but what was unknown could still cause devastating damage and casualties.

If a single missile warhead were filled with anthrax, an infectious animal disease that can spread to humans, "millions of lethal doses could be spread in an attack on any city of the region," he said.

Little progress was made in reporting the whereabouts of such biological warfare agents as aflatoxin, associated with fungal contaminated food grains and known for inducing liver cancer. The report said Iraq's declarations on destruction of the agent " was not supported by sufficient evidence.
But he did not disclose any major arms programmes or materials discovered in the last six months.
Much of the information on past programmes the inspectors have found or questioned came from governments who had delivered materials to Iraq for its past programmes.

But Ekeus said "a small number" of governments, which he did not name, had not responded to repeated and long-standing requests for information. He said it would be "most unfortunate" if this prevented the commission from being able to give Iraq clearance required for any lifting of sanctions.
